newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Senate probe opposes Australian Telstra float.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Senate probe opposes Australian Telstra float.

text.p: An Australian Senate inquiry into the partial float of government-owned telecoms carrier Telstra recommended against the sale on Monday, as expected.
A Senate committee said in a report that it found no substantial evidence to back the Australian government's claim that the economy and consumers would benefit from the sale.
The committee was dominated by non-government parties and its opposition to the sale was expected.

"The Senate committee report, tabled this afternoon, has shown the government's decision to sell Telstra is driven more by economic fashion than fact," the committee said in a statement. "The committee found intense community feeling against partial or full privatisation of Telstra."

The committee said there should be no link between the Telstra sale and environment funding. The government plans to raise A$8 billion through the sale with A$1 billion of the proceeds helping to fund an environmental protection package.
"The committee was of the view that environment programs should be funded in their own right," it said.
The committee also said it believed the Telstra bill should be split into two - one dealing with the sale of Telstra and the other involving its customer service obligations.
"It will leave the Senate dealing with a good bill/bad bill situation, making the issues before the chamber much more clear cut," it said.
The committee said if parliament passed the legislation, the sale should be delayed until December 1998 or at least 18 months after the 1997 deregulation of the telecommunications industry.
However, Communications Minister Richard Alston said it was clear the bulk of the report's evidence was in favour of at least a partial privatisation of Telstra.
"The majority of the report is a disappointing mish-mash of inaccuracies and tired old prejudices," Alston told reporters.
"In many ways it is a very cynical charade because the majority of the members of that committee went in with closed minds."
He said more than half of the submissions received by the committee did not relate to the issue of privatisation.
"There were very many one page submissions from Telstra employees whose concerns had been no doubt agitated by political campaigning," Alston said.
"And there were a number of other submissions that overwhelmingly supported the privatisation proposal, certainly in terms of competition and efficiency," Alston said.
The privatisation would involve one-third of Telstra and the government has repeatedly said it would sell no more without seeking a mandate in an election.
Independent Senators Brian Harradine and Mal Colston hold the key to the passing of the Telstra privatisation bill because the government needs two votes to pass any legisation in the senate.
All other non-government Senators are opposed to the Telstra sale.
